## Tea, bourbons and a Thursday afternoon

When I retired, after 41 years of bookkeeping, mostly for a builders’ merchant in Dereham, I discovered that I was rather short of reasons to leave the house. I drifted along like that for about eighteen months. I was not looking for a worthy cause or a new purpose in life. I simply needed something regular to do.

In March 2022, I started on the Thursday tea trolley in the day therapy unit at Wensum Vale Hospice. It has turned out to suit me very well, although my first week might not have suggested a promising future. I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much that she had to be given a tissue, and told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. This was kind of her, if not entirely reassuring about my trolley skills.

People sometimes assume that volunteering at a hospice must be either harrowing or require all sorts of special skills. On the Thursday tea trolley, neither is true. You do not need nursing experience. You need to be able to push a trolley, make tea and coffee, remember who takes what, and listen. My years of keeping ledgers straight have proved unexpectedly useful for the remembering.

The day unit usually sees between 14 and 18 patients on a Thursday. Many come for the art group or hand massage; some come mainly for the company. Most go home afterwards. My part is to go round with the drinks and biscuits, have a chat where one is wanted, and keep out of the way where it isn’t.

Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods each week. The story varies slightly from one telling to the next. I have stopped correcting the dates. The bourbon biscuits always disappear first, although we have now learned to hide a packet for the late group. These are the sorts of operational matters with which a tea trolley volunteer concerns themselves.

For the most part, Thursday is not a sad afternoon. It is often noisy and rather jolly. That may surprise people who have never been into the day unit, but it is the truth. There are hard weeks too, and I would not pretend otherwise. When those days come, the staff look after us as volunteers. You are not expected to manage everything on your own or to know what to say in every situation. Sometimes making the tea properly and staying to listen is enough.

As for me, Thursdays repaired a hole in my week. I have somewhere to be, people I know, and a job that needs doing. I do not consider this especially virtuous. I get a good deal out of it, including the occasional very funny afternoon and more biscuits than is strictly necessary.

We could now do with two more people joining us. There are meant to be six volunteers on the rota and there are currently four. One left over the summer to move to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren, and another has had a knee operation. Consequently, we are a little stretched.

The commitment is **one Thursday a fortnight, from 1.30pm to 4pm**. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, provides an induction lasting about two hours. There is also a short food hygiene course to complete online, which the hospice pays for. You do not need to arrive knowing anything about hospice care.

If you are curious but not convinced, the easiest thing is to come to the **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, and no obligation to sign up. You can ask questions, find out what is involved and then go home and think about it. If you cannot make that afternoon, or would prefer a chat first, ring Bridget on the volunteering line.

I would be very pleased if at least two readers came along. You need not be a remarkable person, and you certainly need not be a saint. If you can manage a trolley and remember who takes two sugars, you are already most of the way there.
